title: Glossary
intro: A reference for the linguistic terms and concepts used throughout EtymoMap, as well as general terms that are useful for linguistics or terminology used in any of the blog posts.

entries.definition: The comparison of languages to establish their relationships and reconstruct their histories.
The study of word origins and how their forms and meanings have developed over time.
A visual map of a word's ancestry, laid out as a directed acyclic graph of ancestor forms.
A sound law describing the systematic consonant shifts from Proto-Indo-European to Proto-Germanic, setting the Germanic languages apart from the rest of Indo-European.
The study of how languages change over time.
A language used as a common means of communication between speakers of different native languages.
A newly coined word or expression.
The process of inferring unattested earlier forms of a language by comparing its descendants and applying known sound changes. Reconstructed words are conventionally prefixed with an asterisk (*).
A regular, systematic change in pronunciation that applies across a language over time.
A shortened written form of a word or phrase.
A bound morpheme attached to a word to modify its meaning or grammatical function.
Forming a shorter word by removing a real or perceived affix from a longer word.
Shortening a word to a shorter form, such as ad from advertisement.
A word formed by combining two or more existing words.
An affix that surrounds the base on both sides.
Forming a new word by adding affixes or making other changes to an existing word.
Naming something after a person or place.
An abbreviation formed from the initial letters of words and pronounced letter by letter.
A word that imitates the sound it names.
A word formed by merging parts of two or more words.
An affix placed before the base of a word.
The core morpheme that carries a word's primary meaning.
An affix placed after the base of a word.
A borrowing formed by translating the individual elements of a foreign expression.
Interaction between languages that produces borrowing and structural convergence.
A word re-imported from a classical language with little change to its form.
A word adopted from another language.
A loanword that keeps the spelling of the source language.
A borrowing chosen to match both the sound and meaning of native material.
Borrowing only a meaning from another language, without the word's form.
A borrowing that has been partially adapted to the receiving language's patterns.
A loanword retained in close to its original foreign form.
A major language family of northern Africa and the Middle East, including Arabic, Hebrew, and Amharic.
An earlier language from which a later language descends.
A major language family spread across Southeast Asia and the Pacific, including Malay, Tagalog, and Hawaiian.
An intermediate grouping of languages within a family.
A branch of the Indo-European family including Irish, Welsh, Scottish Gaelic, and Breton.
Words in different languages that descend from a common ancestor.
A later language that developed from an earlier one.
Two words in one language that come from the same source by different routes.
A major language family of southern India, including Tamil, Telugu, Kannada, and Malayalam.
An extinct subgroup of the Germanic languages, the best attested of which is Gothic.
The hierarchical genealogy showing how the members of a language family descend from one another.
A branch of the Indo-European family including English, German, Dutch, and the Scandinavian languages.
A large language family spanning much of Europe and parts of Asia, including the Germanic, Romance, Slavic, Celtic, Greek, and Indo-Iranian branches.
A group of languages descended from a common ancestor.
The deepest shared branching point between two languages in a family tree.
A major language family of sub-Saharan Africa, including Swahili, Yoruba, and Zulu.
A subgroup of the Germanic languages including the Scandinavian languages, such as Danish, Swedish, Norwegian, and Icelandic.
The reconstructed common ancestor of the Germanic languages.
The reconstructed common ancestor of the Indo-European language family.
The reconstructed common ancestor of the Italic languages, including Latin.
A reconstructed ancestral language from which a family descends.
The reconstructed common ancestor of the Romance languages, essentially the spoken (Vulgar) Latin of late antiquity, as distinct from the literary Classical Latin.
The reconstructed common ancestor of the West Germanic languages, including English, German, Dutch, and Frisian.
A branch of the Indo-European family descended from Latin, including French, Spanish, Italian, Portuguese, and Romanian.
A major language family of East Asia, including Chinese (Mandarin), Burmese, and Tibetan.
A branch of the Indo-European family including Russian, Polish, Czech, and the South Slavic languages.
A language family native to northern Eurasia, including Finnish, Hungarian, and Estonian.
A subgroup of the Germanic languages including English, German, Dutch, and Frisian.
A trait shared across languages because of geographic proximity rather than common descent.
The spread of a language or linguistic feature across space and time.
A word transmitted naturally down a language's own line of descent.
Languages becoming more similar to one another through sustained contact.
A region where unrelated languages come to share structural features through contact.
The standard system for transcribing the sounds of spoken language.
The smallest unit of sound in a language that can distinguish one word from another.
The written representation of a word's pronunciation using IPA.
The way a word is spoken.
The study of the geographic distribution of languages.
A unique identifier assigned to every language in the Glottolog database.
The region where a language historically originated.
The geographic area where a language is spoken.
The canonical citation form of a word.
The evolution of a word's meaning over time.
